title: Calleja v. Executive Secretary
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020 in most of its provisions but declared certain provisions unconstitutional, including the designation power of the Anti-Terrorism Council and the penalty for publishing certain content.
doctrine: The Anti-Terrorism Act is constitutional in proscribing terrorism but certain provisions are unconstitutional. The designation of individuals as terrorists by the ATC without judicial authorization violates due process. Provisions penalizing those who publish content inciting terrorism are overbroad and violate freedom of expression.
fullText:
LEONEN, J.:

These consolidated petitions challenge the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 11479, the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020.

The law defines terrorism as engaging in acts intended to cause death, serious bodily injury, or extensive destruction or damage to property, government facilities, public utilities, or critical infrastructure when the purpose is to intimidate the general public, create an atmosphere of fear, or seriously destabilize the fundamental political, economic, or social structures of the country.

While the State has a compelling interest in combating terrorism, the means employed must not be overbroad or vague as to chill protected freedoms. Certain provisions of the law fail this test.
